passage:
Tuesday night, 11 pm. Today Wasim solved the maths problem that had stumped me, and I felt irritated, not impressed. I actually thought the words "scholarship kid" in my head. At the canteen I took the bench he was heading for and pretended not to see. When Rakesh joked about Wasim wearing the same shoes all term, I laughed too.
Now I can't sleep. My driver drops me at the gate each morning. Wasim takes two buses and still turns in every worksheet. I have a tutor; he has a library card, and he beat me anyway.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask him how he solved it, and mean it.
Suraj

qa.q: How does Wasim get to school?
qa.a: He takes two buses.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Wasim solved the maths problem, and what does he feel later?
qa.a: He was irritated rather than impressed, and by night he feels uneasy about his own thought, 'scholarship kid', and about laughing along.

qa.q: What could Suraj do differently tomorrow?
qa.a: He could ask Wasim how he solved the problem and truly listen, treating Wasim as a classmate for who he is.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when Suraj took the bench and others joked about his shoes?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt left out and judged before anyone knew him, even though he works hard and turns in every worksheet.

grounding: A boy with money notices his contempt for a scholarship classmate, sees how privilege shapes him, and resolves to treat the classmate as a person.

passage:
"Ma, please move the sewing machine to the back room before Lalremsiami comes."
"Why? That machine pays your school fees."
"It's just... our room is so small. Everyone else has sofas."
The bell rang.
"Damini! Is that your mother's work? That blouse is gorgeous. Could she stitch one for my cousin's wedding?"
Damini stared. "You don't mind... the room?"
"Mind? It smells like tea and it's cosy. Any chance of a cup?"
Ma laughed and put the kettle on.
Later Damini whispered, "Sorry, Ma."
"Work is honest work, beta. Nothing to hide."

qa.q: What does Damini's mother use to pay for school fees?
qa.a: Her sewing machine pays the school fees.

qa.q: Why did Damini ask her mother to move the sewing machine?
qa.a: She was ashamed of the small room and worried how it would look to a friend, since everyone else has sofas.

qa.q: What can Damini take from Lalremsiami's reaction?
qa.a: That a true friend cares about her and admires the work, not the house, so the shame can loosen and she can be prouder of her mother's skill. 🙂

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see the room and Damini's mother?
qa.a: She finds the room cosy and admires the blouse so much that she asks for one for her cousin's wedding.

grounding: Damini is ashamed of her mother's sewing work and small home when a friend visits; the friend's warm reaction and her mother's words show dignity of work.

passage:
I'm Tenzin, and I was fourteen when I first heard my parents arguing behind the kitchen door about the loan and my school fees. Ama said, "We'll manage." Papa said, "With what?"
I lay awake that night. I decided to stop asking for a new geometry box, and I even planned to quit tuition without telling anyone. I felt like a bill the family had to pay.
Binita, my little sister, found me staring at the ceiling and said nothing, just sat beside me.
That weekend I asked Ama, "What's happening with the money?" She sat down and said it was a hard season, and not mine to solve. I could help by telling her my worries instead of hiding them. I was still scared, but I wasn't alone with it.

qa.q: What were Tenzin's parents arguing about behind the kitchen door?
qa.a: They were arguing about the loan and Tenzin's school fees.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin feel like a bill the family had to pay?
qa.a: Tenzin overheard the fight about fees and felt guilty for costing money, so decided to stop asking for a geometry box and to quit tuition.

qa.q: What did asking Ama help Tenzin see, and what could Tenzin do next?
qa.a: It showed the money trouble was not Tenzin's to solve, so Tenzin can keep sharing worries with Ama and help within a child's role.

qa.q: How might Ama have seen Tenzin's question about the money?
qa.a: Ama may have seen that Tenzin was worrying silently, so she sat down and explained it was a hard season that Tenzin did not need to fix.

grounding: A teen overhears parents arguing about debts and fees, feels scared and guilty, asks what is happening, and learns a child is not the fixer.

passage:
I'm Irawati. Last year Papa kept saying, "No tension, beta, all is well." But he stopped taking the scooter and walked to work, and twice I saw the shop's shutter down early. My brother Asif told me not to ask.
I felt so protected that I felt shut out. Guessing was worse than knowing.
One night I said, "Papa, I'm sixteen. I can handle hearing it. I'm not asking you to fix anything." He was quiet for a while, and then he admitted the shop had been slow for months.
I stopped mentioning the class trip and told him I'd manage with my old phone. I didn't blame him. I just said I'd rather know than guess, and he nodded.

qa.q: What did Irawati notice about how Papa got to work?
qa.a: He stopped taking the scooter and walked to work.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel about being protected from the truth?
qa.a: She felt shut out, because guessing at what was wrong was harder for her than knowing.

qa.q: How did Irawati adjust her asks without blaming Papa?
qa.a: She stopped mentioning the class trip and said she would manage with her old phone, telling Papa she would rather know than guess.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Irawati said she could handle hearing it?
qa.a: After a quiet pause he admitted the shop had been slow, so he may have felt relieved to stop pretending, though probably still worried.

grounding: A parent hides a money problem to protect the teen, who senses it, kindly asks for honesty and adjusts her requests without blame.

passage:
"Irawati, put the phone down and listen to your Masi Sarika. When I was fifteen, three friends came back from the hill station with photos and brand-new phones. I smiled at them, then went home and slammed the cupboard door. I was bitter, truly.
I even thought of asking the shopkeeper for a phone on instalment behind Ma's back.
Then I stood in the kitchen and said out loud, 'I'm jealous.' It felt smaller once it was said. I counted what I had: a bicycle, a friend who lent me stories, a mother who made poori on Sundays.
I told my friends I couldn't afford the trip. Nobody laughed. The feeling came back sometimes, but it always passed."

qa.q: What did Sarika think of asking the shopkeeper for?
qa.a: She thought of asking for a phone on instalment behind Ma's back.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after her friends came back from the hill station?
qa.a: She was bitter and jealous: she smiled at them, but slammed the cupboard door when she got home.

qa.q: What would you advise a teenager who feels envy about a friend's new things?
qa.a: They can say the feeling aloud as Sarika did, count what they have, and avoid pretending or borrowing to keep up. 🙂

qa.q: How might Irawati take her Masi's story?
qa.a: Irawati may find it reassuring that envy is normal and passes, since Masi Sarika tells it while Irawati is busy on her phone.

grounding: An elder recalls envy of friends' new phones and trips, admitting the bitterness, counting what she had and not borrowing to keep up.

qa.q: What is Ishita worried about, and what does she want her plan to do?

qa.q: What steps does Pranav suggest for Ishita?
qa.a: He suggests asking Mrs. Kulkarni about the Class 11 scholarship and trying small, safe weekend tutoring, with school staying first.

qa.q: What would change if Ishita never told her parents?

grounding: Ishita considers leaving school for work to help with fees; a friend nudges her to discuss with family and a teacher and look for a scholarship and small safe earning.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Monday. At the lockers I overheard a boy ask Amandeep, "Nice book. Whose grandad did it belong to?" Others laughed. Amandeep's cheeks reddened, but he answered calmly, "It was my cousin's, and it still has every page." Then he went quiet for the rest of the break.
I asked him to stay after class. He said it was fine, and that he didn't want a fuss. I told him a book or a uniform says nothing about a person's worth, and that he should come to me if it keeps happening. I spoke to the boy privately and changed the seating.
Chandrika, who has a second-hand set herself, sat with Amandeep at lunch.
Mr. Dsouza

qa.q: What did the boy ask Amandeep about his book?
qa.a: He asked whose grandad the book had belonged to.

qa.q: What might Amandeep be feeling after the remark, even though he replied calmly?
qa.a: He is probably hurt and embarrassed: his cheeks reddened and he went quiet for the rest of the break.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do if the teasing keeps happening?
qa.a: He can keep answering calmly and tell Mr. Dsouza again, remembering that a book or uniform says nothing about his worth.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt seeing this?
qa.a: Since Chandrika has a second-hand set too, she probably understood the sting, and sitting with Amandeep at lunch shows her support.

grounding: A classmate teases Amandeep about second-hand books; he replies calmly and the teacher affirms his dignity and deals with the teasing.

passage:
At the community centre's computer corner, Keerthana's phone buzzed with a message from an unknown number: "Work from home, earn big every day. Just pay a small registration fee first."
Her family's shop had been struggling, and her pulse quickened. She showed it to Sahil, who was printing his project. "Sounds too easy," he said. "My cousin got one like that and never saw the money again."
The fee was small. She had that much in her purse. Mrs. Nair, who helps at the centre, looked at the screen. "Anyone who asks you to pay first in order to earn is a warning sign. Don't send anything. Show this to your parents tonight, and block the number."
Keerthana let out a breath. "I really wanted it to be true."

qa.q: What did the message ask Keerthana to pay first?
qa.a: It asked her to pay a small registration fee first.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling, and why did the offer tempt her?
qa.a: She felt hopeful but unsure: her family's shop had been struggling, so she really wanted the offer to be true.

qa.q: What should Keerthana do now?
qa.a: She should send nothing, block the number and show the message to her parents, as Mrs. Nair advised.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the offer?
qa.a: Sahil sees it as too easy to be real, because his cousin got a similar message and never saw the money again.

grounding: A quick-money message tempts a teen in a struggling family; the adult and friend help her recognise it and not send money.

In the school office, Darshan Mama slid the fee receipt across the counter. "Third term, and again from my pocket," he told the clerk, loud enough for the queue to hear. "Family must help family."
Urmila stood beside him, her face warm. She was grateful, she really was. She also wanted the floor to open.
"Thank you, Mama," she said. "Truly. I'll make it count, and one day I'll pay it back."
He smiled and patted her head as if that settled it.
At home she asked Amma, "Could you tell Mama we're thankful, but he needn't say it in front of people?"
Amma sighed. "I'll talk to him gently. He means well, but we should say something."
Urmila went back to her homework, still feeling two things at once.

qa.q: What did Darshan Mama tell the clerk?
qa.a: He said it was the third term and again from his pocket, and that family must help family.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Urmila have in the office?
qa.a: She felt grateful, but she was also humiliated and wanted the floor to open.

qa.q: What could Urmila and her parents do about the reminders?
qa.a: Urmila can keep thanking Mama sincerely and plan to repay him one day, while Amma gently asks him not to mention the fees in public.

qa.q: How might Darshan Mama see his remark to the clerk?
qa.a: He may see it as ordinary family duty said with a good heart, without noticing that it embarrasses Urmila.

grounding: A relative pays the fees and reminds everyone of it; the teen feels gratitude and humiliation, thanks him and asks her parent to set a gentle boundary.

passage:
The power went out at nine, the night before the science test. Nirmala carried her books to the doorstep, where the streetlight fell. Inside, her mother was counting coins for the milk money again, and the clink stayed in Nirmala's head.
I will never count coins like that, she thought, and read the same page faster.
Then the uglier thought came: it was her parents' fault. She stopped. Her mother had been on her feet since five.
Her brother Tenzin came out with a torch and sat on the step. "Want me to quiz you?"
She let the drive carry her through the chapter. When Tenzin fell asleep against her shoulder, she covered him with her shawl and read on.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala move her books when the power went out?
qa.a: She moved them to the doorstep, where the streetlight fell.

qa.q: What ugly thought did Nirmala catch, and why did she stop?
qa.a: She caught herself blaming her parents, and stopped when she remembered her mother had been on her feet since five.

qa.q: How can Nirmala use her money stress in a healthy way?
qa.a: She can let it fuel her studying, as she does with the chapter, while reminding herself that her family is not to blame.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin in this scene?
qa.a: Tenzin wants to help, bringing a torch and offering to quiz her, and trusts her enough to fall asleep against her shoulder.

grounding: Money stress fuels a teen's drive to succeed while she refuses to blame her family for being poor.
